headline: Funding flows. Launch targets. Data centers proliferate.
deck: This week saw significant funding rounds and ambitious launch plans, alongside a new wave of satellite data center proposals.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M for co-orbital security
stories.body: True Anomaly secured a $190M Series C round, bringing its valuation to $1.6B. The funding will bolster its efforts in co-orbital security and space domain awareness, which are becoming essential as geopolitical tensions rise. This cash influx suggests that the DoD is prioritizing partnerships with established players rather than taking risks on unproven startups.
stories.soWhat: In a market where familiarity often trumps novelty, True Anomaly's success underscores the defense sector's preference for known quantities over experimental technologies.

stories.head: SSC Space and Firefly target 2028 for Sweden launch
stories.body: SSC Space and Firefly are aiming for their first orbital launch from Esrange, Sweden, by 2028. This ambitious timeline reflects a growing interest in European launch capabilities, particularly as the region seeks to reduce reliance on established players like SpaceX. However, given the track record of ambitious timelines in the space industry, skepticism is warranted.
stories.soWhat: If they miss this target, it could further entrench the notion that European launch initiatives are more about aspiration than execution.

stories.head: Orbital plans to launch 100,000 data center satellites
stories.body: Startup Orbital announced plans to deploy 100,000 satellites for data centers to meet the surging demand for AI processing. The scale of this proposal raises eyebrows, as it could exacerbate the already pressing issue of space debris. With the current regulatory environment, one has to wonder how they plan to navigate the bureaucratic maze to make this a reality.
stories.soWhat: If Orbital succeeds, we might soon be swimming in space junk, which could make the term 'data center' take on a whole new meaning.

watchlist.title: Keep an eye on the ESA lunar mapping bid
watchlist.body: The European Space Agency's search for lunar mapping capabilities could signal a new phase in lunar exploration, with implications for both commercial and governmental projects.

watchlist.title: Watch for updates on hypersonic glide-vehicle tests
watchlist.body: With the latest tests slipping again, the implications for defense readiness and technology development could be significant, particularly for funding allocations.

watchlist.title: Palantir's TITAN program extension
watchlist.body: The $480M extension for Palantir's TITAN program indicates continued government reliance on established tech firms for critical infrastructure.

watchlist.title: Potential fallout from Russian co-orbital activity
watchlist.body: Increased Russian activity near commercial GEO slots might prompt a reevaluation of risk assessments by insurers and could lead to a tightening of compliance measures.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
